analysis.one_liner: Requires air toxics monitoring at industrial fence lines and deploys over 1,000 community air sensors.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2022 with 6 Senate cosponsors, the bill never got a committee hearing or a vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to monitor hazardous air pollutants at the fence lines of at least 100 high-priority industrial facilities — many of them chemical, petrochemical, and petroleum plants — publish the results quickly and in multiple languages, and set enforceable 'corrective action levels' that trigger cleanup and a public violation report when pollution crosses them. It also would have added 80 multipollutant monitoring stations and at least 100 reference monitors to the national air network, prioritizing neighborhoods with high asthma, cancer, or poverty rates, and deployed at least 1,000 low-cost air sensors in communities affected by pollution. It authorized roughly $277 million for fiscal years 2023–24. It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near industrial facilities that emit hazardous air pollutants like ethylene oxide, chloroprene, benzene, and formaldehyde — the bill named census tracts with elevated cancer risk, poverty, or disease rates as priorities for new monitors and sensors. Communities nearest these plants, which are disproportionately lower-income, would gain real-time public data on what they are breathing and enforceable trigger points for cleanup.

how_it_helps.text: Required fenceline monitoring at no fewer than 100 high-priority sources of hazardous air pollutants, including facilities flagged by EPA's Inspector General as contributing to high local cancer risk [S3].
Made monitoring data public within 7 days of submission, in multiple languages, with community-wide alerts when emissions exceed health reference levels [S3].

Set enforceable corrective action levels at fence lines: exceeding one triggers a root-cause analysis, remedial action to protect the most exposed residents, and a public report that a Clean Air Act violation occurred [S3].

Required at least 40 of 80 new multipollutant monitoring stations to be sited in census tracts with above-average asthma, COPD, heart disease, cancer, poverty, unemployment, or multiple nearby major pollution sources [S3].
Deployed no fewer than 1,000 low-cost air sensors (under $5,000 each) in clusters of at least 5 in affected communities, with residents invited to propose sensor sites [S3].
Allowed satellite data to be used in determining whether areas violate national air quality standards, so pollution can be documented even where ground monitors are sparse [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of petroleum, chemical, petrochemical, plastics, metals, and related facilities, who would have to install and maintain continuous emissions and fenceline monitoring equipment, meet 95% data reliability requirements, repair broken monitors within 2 days, and take corrective action when pollution exceeds health-based levels. Taxpayers would fund roughly $277 million in EPA monitoring programs for fiscal years 2023–24. Some compliance costs could be passed through to consumers in the form of higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Industrial facilities bear the full cost of installing and maintaining continuous emissions and fenceline monitoring systems, keeping that data 95% reliable, and repairing failures within 2 days, with no exemptions [S3].

Exceeding a corrective action level is treated as a Clean Air Act violation with mandatory remediation and public reporting, exposing facilities to penalties and enforcement costs beyond the price of the monitors themselves [S3].

New monitors that show a previously 'in attainment' area actually violates a national standard would force redesignation of that area as nonattainment within 2 years, which can restrict industrial expansion and trigger stricter permitting in the affected region [S3].

Low-cost sensors cost no more than $5,000 each and can be less accurate than reference monitors; the bill only requires EPA to install reference monitors where sensor data reaches 98% of a standard, and allows EPA to waive that requirement on 'clear and convincing evidence' the sensors were inaccurate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people living next to major air toxics sources, the benefits are direct: publicly available, near-real-time data on what chemicals are crossing their property line, and an automatic trigger for investigation and cleanup when levels get dangerous. The costs fall mainly on the regulated industries and on the federal budget (~$277 million over two years). The bill is a monitoring and enforcement bill more than an emission-cutting mandate — it does not directly cap emissions — but by making violations public and enforceable it creates pressure to reduce pollution. The main design weaknesses are the accuracy limits of cheap sensors and the fact that only 100 priority sources would be monitored initially.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Duckworth introduced the Public Health Air Quality Act of 2022 on July 12, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1] [S5].
Six Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].

The action history shows no further activity after the July 12, 2022 referral — no hearings, markup, or floor vote — and the bill received no consideration before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Petroleum, petrochemical, and chemical facilities are better off: they face no new fenceline monitoring requirements, corrective action levels, or public violation reports. Communities near those facilities gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Tammy Duckworth
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired at the time by Sen. Tom Carper (D-DE)
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up after referral — no hearing or markup is recorded — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: As chair, did not schedule the bill for committee consideration during the remainder of the 117th Congress.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no Republican support in a chamber where 50 Republicans held seats.

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters — the sponsor and six cosponsors — were Democrats; none of the 50 Senate Republicans signed on, and a Democratic-held committee declined to advance it.

industries.note: The bill targeted NAICS codes including 324 and 325, requiring continuous and fenceline monitoring, corrective action levels for the top carcinogens, and public violation reports when exceeded. Refineries and petrochemical plants near fenceline communities would bear the heaviest compliance and enforcement exposure; its defeat left current monitoring rules in place.

Facilities in NAICS 322, 325, 326, 331, 332, and 339 emitting ethylene oxide, chloroprene, benzene, formaldehyde, or metal compounds would have needed emissions measurement systems and risk management plan monitoring. They avoid those costs because the bill died.

industries.industry: Air monitoring and sensor equipment manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have mandated 80 NCore stations, at least 100 reference monitors, and 1,000+ air sensors costing up to $5,000 each, a sizable government purchase of monitoring hardware. The mandate lapsed with the bill.

Some facilities in these codes fell within the bill's monitoring criteria; they would have gained from cleanup and remediation contracts triggered by corrective actions but faced their own monitoring and reporting obligations.
